docs.title: About this adaptation
docs.text:
This lesson borrows and adapts the starter template from the Hugging Face Agents Course. Because API access, model availability, and hosting requirements affected the original setup, this version runs locally and uses Groq for model calls. It still uses Hugging Face's smolagents Python library.

Image generation has been removed. The Week 2 core practical uses two tools: timezone lookup and web search. Creating your own tool is optional in Week 2 and becomes a guided required exercise in Week 03.

The learning material and executable instructions are provided on this local site. External HF lesson pages are optional references. Weeks 1–2 retain the two quick quizzes; the account-gated final quiz and certification are not part of this adaptation.

During our original setup, free Space duplication was unavailable and HF inference later returned a no-credit error. A local interface does not make remote inference unlimited. Use your own Groq key and check current usage limits.

docs.title: Course route
docs.text:
New to terminals or editing Python? Read Before you start first. It explains which window to use, how to locate files, and how to save edits.

  1. Week 1 — understand and trace the loop: read agent foundations, complete the two quick quizzes, prepare your local environment, and build the three-stage dummy agent.
  2. Week 2 — run and extend a working agent: run the template, understand its components, enable and verify tools, and complete the practical checks.
  3. Week 03 — create terminal-based agents: follow the setup and file-creation steps, run your programs, modify function/class tools, and build Agentic RAG. Agent teams and vision/browser topics continue in Week 04.

See the course route for learning objectives and the evidence to bring to each week's review.

The full template comes after the dummy exercise. Students first see how a model call, a function, and an observation fit together; then CodeAgent automates that loop.

See the Week 1 plan →

The quick-quiz links open the original activities. All other steps can be followed using this local guide.

Use the supplied local starter for executable edits. Complete the response and tool checkpoints on your machine; changing provider/model can change behavior.

docs.title: Model compatibility update
docs.text: The earlier GPT-OSS configuration returned “Tool choice is none, but model called a tool” during a live test. The course's CodeAgent expects Python code in text; a native API function call is a different format. Groq documents this possible tool-choice rejection. The updated starter uses Qwen 3.8 27B with reasoning disabled and explicit code-format instructions. It is currently a preview model with free-plan limits; availability and behavior must be checked before class.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: This walkthrough explains setup from the beginning. The later practical expects you to recognize a Python function, its arguments, and its return value. For a refresher, read the Python guide to defining functions, including arguments and return values. You do not need previous experience building agents.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Windows PC or Mac, a browser, and an internet connection.
  • Permission to install Python and a code editor. On a managed computer, use its approved software portal; if installation is restricted, use a computer where you have installation permission.
  • Your own Groq account for model calls. No HF token, final quiz, or certificate is needed for the practical.
  • A plain-text/code editor. If you already have one, keep using it. You can install Visual Studio Code and open your exercise folder with File → Open Folder.

The local app still contacts remote services. Working installations can encounter model availability, permissions, or credit limits. An error at that stage is not necessarily a mistake in your code.

docs.title: Know which window to use
docs.text:
Window What goes there Terminal on Mac / Command Prompt on Windows Commands such as python app.py Code editor Changes to app.py and other project files Browser Account settings, this guide, quizzes, and the running agent's chat

Never paste terminal commands into the agent chat. Never paste your token into the chat or a Python source file.

docs.title: Open a command window
docs.text:
Mac: press Command + Space, type Terminal, and press Return.

Windows: open Start, type Command Prompt, and open it. Use Command Prompt for this guide, not PowerShell.

Copy only the text inside a command block, or use its copy button. Do not copy the surrounding triple backticks, an example prompt, or output. Run one command at a time and wait until the prompt returns before the next command.

(.venv) is part of a prompt, not a command. >>> means you opened the Python interpreter; type exit() and press Enter/Return to get back to your normal command window.

docs.title: Find your downloaded project
docs.text:
During the dummy exercise, work in agent-course/dummy-agent and create dummy_agent.py there. Later, after downloading the first-agent starter, use this separate folder:

agent-course/
└── First_agent_template/
    ├── app.py
    ├── Gradio_UI.py
    ├── prompts.yaml
    ├── requirements.txt
    ├── tools/
    └── .venv/              (created during setup; may be hidden)

Other files may also be present. Edit the project files, not files inside .venv.

Mac: in Finder, choose Go → Go to Folder, enter ~/agent-course/First_agent_template, and press Return.

Windows: enter %USERPROFILE%\agent-course\First_agent_template in File Explorer's address bar and press Enter.

In your editor, use File → Open Folder (if available) to open that folder. Select a file from its file list. Double-clicking a .py file in the file manager may run it instead of opening it for editing.

docs.title: Edit a file without losing your place
docs.text:
1. Open the named file in your editor.
  2. Use Find (Command + F on Mac or Control + F on Windows) to locate the exact text in the guide.
  3. Replace only that line or block. Keep its leading spaces, commas, and surrounding parentheses.
  4. Save with Command + S or Control + S. Keep the original extension: app.py, not app.py.txt.
  5. Return to the terminal, stop the app with Control + C if it is running, and start it again.
  6. Refresh the app's browser page.

Do not use a word processor to edit Python. Indentation is part of Python's structure; keep the spacing shown in code examples.

docs.title: If you get stuck
docs.text:
Stop at the first failing step rather than continuing with later commands. Note the step number and the command you ran. Copy the error from the terminal, excluding any credentials, then match the error to troubleshooting. Check your current folder, active environment, and the exact command before retrying.

For a running app, the terminal stays occupied: this is expected. To run another command there, first stop the app with Control + C. On a Mac, this is the Control key, not Command.

docs.title: Dummy agent: build the loop in three stages
docs.text:
This local exercise adapts the manual-loop idea from the HF Dummy Agent lesson. All code needed is below. The original page is optional reading; Groq replaces its model connection.

You will send a request, inspect a proposed action, execute a function yourself, and send its result back. This is a teaching example, not a general-purpose autonomous agent. The full template comes later.

docs.title: Where does the weather information come from?
docs.text:
Stage What actually happens Weather information Step 1 The model answers a general question No weather request or function call Step 2 The model writes a proposed action as text No function has run; any weather it invents is unverified Step 3 Your Python program calls get_weather("London") The function returns fixed demo data: sunny, 18°C

In Step 3, you add get_weather to the same dummy_agent.py file. Its return line contains sunny, 18 degrees Celsius. We chose those values for the exercise; they are not measurements or a live forecast. Python sends that returned string to the model, which uses it to write the final response.

If you have an older script whose prompt says “invent an example weather result,” that is a text-only simulation. The model invents its weather, and no Python weather function runs. Use the three stages below together in a new file; do not append them to a different older script.

docs.title: Prepare the file
docs.text:
Complete basic setup and activate the environment in agent-course/dummy-agent. In your editor, create dummy_agent.py in that folder. Add the blocks below in order to this one file, saving after each stage. After pasting and saving the Step 1 code, run:

python dummy_agent.py

Output appears in the terminal, not a browser chat. Each rerun repeats the requests already in your file and uses your Groq allowance. If you reach a limit, follow the provider's retry interval rather than repeatedly rerunning.

docs.title: Step 1. Make a simple LLM call
docs.text:
Put this in the new file:

from getpass import getpass
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.groq.com/openai/v1",
    api_key=getpass("Paste your Groq API key (hidden): ").strip(),
)
MODEL = "qwen/qwen3.8-27b"

reply = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=MODEL,
    reasoning_effort="none",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Name the capital city of France."}],
    max_tokens=150,
)
print("STEP 1 — model response:")
print(reply.choices[0].message.content)

Save and run it. Paste your key into the hidden terminal prompt and press Enter/Return.

What happens: messages supplies the user request. The client sends it to Groq. choices[0].message.content reads the first returned answer. No weather function has run and no agent framework is involved.

Checkpoint: You receive an answer identifying Paris. This tests the model connection. A traceback is a connection or request problem; use troubleshooting before continuing.

docs.title: Step 2. Inspect a proposed action
docs.text:
Append this block below Step 1:

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are demonstrating a text-based action loop.
The available capability is get_weather(location: str).
Describe an action as plain text, not a native API function call.
Use these labels in order:
Action: get_weather(location="city name")
Observation: the result supplied by the Python program
Final Answer: a brief answer using that result
Do not claim that an observation came from a real function unless supplied.
"""
weather_messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Use get_weather to check the weather in London."},
]

proposal = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=MODEL,
    reasoning_effort="none",
    messages=weather_messages,
    max_tokens=250,
)
print("STEP 2A — without a stop marker:")
print(proposal.choices[0].message.content)

stopped_reply = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=MODEL,
    reasoning_effort="none",
    messages=weather_messages,
    max_tokens=250,
    stop=["Observation:"],
)
proposed_action = stopped_reply.choices[0].message.content or ""
print("STEP 2B — stop before the observation:")
print(proposed_action)

Save and rerun. You will enter the key again. Compare the two outputs.

What happens: the system message describes a capability, but it does not execute it. Without a stop marker, the model might invent a result, state that a result is missing, or simply stop. Do not expect identical wording on every run. The stop parameter stops generation if the model reaches the specified marker, reserving that point for feedback from your program.

Checkpoint: Inspect Step 2B for a proposed get_weather action with London as the input. It should not contain a claimed function result. If it names a different action or city, fix the prompt before proceeding. A stop marker alone does not guarantee the model follows every instruction.

docs.title: Step 3. Execute the function and return its observation
docs.text:
Append this block below Step 2:

def get_weather(location: str) -> str:
    """Return fixed demonstration data, not a live weather forecast."""
    return f"Demo weather for {location}: sunny, 18 degrees Celsius."

# Read Step 2B first. This teaching script handles only the London example.
confirmation = input("Does Step 2B request get_weather for London? Type yes: ")
if confirmation.strip().lower() != "yes":
    raise SystemExit("Check the proposed action and prompt before running the function.")

observation = get_weather("London")
print("STEP 3 — actual Python function result:")
print(observation)

follow_up = weather_messages + [
    {"role": "assistant", "content": proposed_action},
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": (
            "Observation from the Python function: " + observation
            + "\nNow give a final answer. Clearly label this as demo data."
        ),
    },
]
final_reply = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=MODEL,
    reasoning_effort="none",
    messages=follow_up,
    max_tokens=250,
)
print("STEP 3 — model answer using the observation:")
print(final_reply.choices[0].message.content)

Run Step 3: Save dummy_agent.py and run python dummy_agent.py again in the same activated terminal. The earlier stages run again first. Enter your key, read the output labelled STEP 2B, then type yes only if it proposes get_weather for London. Step 3 then prints the function result followed by the model’s final answer.

What happens: you verify the proposed action, Python calls the function, and its return value is added to the next model request. The function returns fixed demonstration data so you can trace where the answer came from. No weather API is contacted.

The confirmation is deliberate: this small script does not parse arbitrary model actions or automatically choose functions. Do not paste the generated text into eval or exec. In the next practical, CodeAgent supplies the execution loop.

Checkpoint: The terminal prints the function result before the final model answer. The answer should reflect the supplied sunny/18-degree demonstration data and identify it as demo data. If it contradicts the observation, inspect the final request and prompt rather than treating the answer as verified.

docs.title: What you have learned
docs.text:
Part Your evidence Model request The first answer came from Groq Proposed action The model named a function and input Execution Your Python script actually called get_weather Observation The returned string entered the next request Final response The model used the supplied result

This weather function is only a dummy example. The full agent's core tools will be real timezone lookup and web search.

Finish Week 1: Review the Week 1 completion checks. You can stop here for this week.

Next week: Follow the Week 2 plan, starting with downloading and running the agent template.

docs.title: Enable and test the template’s tools
docs.text:
Continue with the First_agent_template you already downloaded, set up, and ran in Get the agent template. You should have received a model response and read Understand the template.

Now enable timezone lookup and web search in that working app. Both implementations are supplied. In the required exercise, you test and register them; writing a new tool is optional. Use your existing project folder, its .venv, and your Groq key throughout this practical.

Your required tasks: create the two direct-test files, add the two supplied tools to the agent’s existing tools=[...] list, restart the app, and show successful calls and results in the chat’s execution logs. You do not need to edit Gradio_UI.py or the model connection.

This practical adapts the Hugging Face starter tutorial for our local app.

docs.title: 1. Prepare your existing app for editing
docs.text:
In the terminal running your app, press Control + C to stop it. Leave the template's virtual environment active. Open your existing First_agent_template folder in a code editor and save a copy of app.py as app.before-tools.py for comparison.

After each edit, save the file, run python app.py in that same terminal, enter your Groq key when prompted, and refresh the chat page. Stop the app before making the next change. If returning in a new terminal, use the restart commands to reactivate this project's environment.

docs.title: Files used in this practical
docs.text:
The small test scripts are new files you create during this lesson. They are not in the original starter ZIP. Use the exact name check_time.py (with an underscore), not checktime.py.

File What to do app.py Edit the existing agent program to register tools check_time.py Create beside app.py in Step 3B to test the time function directly check_search.py Create beside app.py in Step 4B to test search directly tools/web_search.py Already supplied; keep it inside the tools folder

Your folder will look like this after creating the two test files:

First_agent_template/
├── app.py
├── check_time.py
├── check_search.py
├── Gradio_UI.py
├── prompts.yaml
├── requirements.txt
├── tools/
│   ├── final_answer.py
│   └── web_search.py
└── .venv/

Keep the test scripts here, not inside tools/ or .venv/. Put each test's code in its own file, not in app.py. Save Python files without an extra .txt extension.

If you already have the completed app.py

The completed reference has both tools registered. Keep its existing tools list. Run the direct tests in 3B and 4B, then the chat tests in 3D and 4D. You can skip the registration edits in 3C and 4C. The optional custom tool is still unfinished.

docs.title: Supplied tools and your edits
docs.text: Already in your template Your work now Working timezone function, not registered Test it directly, register it, and inspect a real agent call Search tool, not registered Test it directly, add an instance, and verify returned sources Custom-tool placeholder, not registered Optional: implement, test, and register your own tool

docs.title: 2. Find the tool registration
docs.text:
Open app.py and find CodeAgent(...) inside main(). Its initial registration is:

tools=[final_answer],

At this point, only final_answer is registered. The time function and search class exist in your files, but the agent cannot call those supplied tools yet. Importing WebSearchTool does not enable web search. If the model produces a web_search(...) call before registration, that call fails; a link from model memory is not a search result.

Keep final_answer in this list. You will add the existing timezone function and a search-tool instance in the next steps. The STUDENT TASK comments mark these edit points. Keep the working model connection and interface settings as they are.

For the optional custom tool later, follow Step 6: create and connect a new tool.

docs.title: How does the agent know which tools it can use?
docs.text:
tools=[...] is the connection between your Python tools and the agent. CodeAgent includes each registered tool's name, description, input descriptions, and types in the instructions sent to the model. The model receives this information together with your chat request and chooses a suitable action.

For example, a request for Tokyo's current time fits the description of get_current_time_in_timezone. A request to find an official website fits web_search. The model generates Python using those names; the local executor runs it. See what CodeAgent handles automatically.

Part Where to edit Purpose Function implementation The function body in app.py, above main() Does the actual work Function description The docstring directly below def Tells the model when to use the tool Input descriptions The docstring's Args: section Helps the model supply suitable arguments Tool registration tools=[...] inside CodeAgent(...) in main() Makes the tool available to this agent

The timezone function is already defined in app.py; it needs registration, not another implementation file. check_time.py only tests it. Search is defined separately in tools/web_search.py: its class has a description field, and the import in app.py makes the class available to your program. Registering WebSearchTool(max_results=3) makes an instance available to the agent.

docs.title: How does it decide when to call a tool?
docs.text:
There is no fixed rule such as “if the user says time, call this function.” The model uses the request and tool descriptions to choose. For a first test, ask explicitly: “Use get_current_time_in_timezone with Asia/Tokyo.” Then inspect the code and execution output. Registration makes a tool available; it does not guarantee the model chooses it or supplies the correct inputs.

prompts.yaml contains general instructions and examples. Some examples mention search or wiki, but examples do not register tools. A generated search(...) call is not a successful search; our registered search tool is named web_search. Use the tools list and the actual execution logs to check what happened.

docs.title: 3. Enable the time-zone tool
docs.text: Goal: make the agent obtain a time from an actual function call and distinguish that result from a model guess.

docs.title: A. Read the function
docs.text:
Find get_current_time_in_timezone in app.py. Its input is a timezone identifier such as Asia/Tokyo. Its output is a string containing the date and time.

Code in the function What it does @tool Wraps the function with metadata the agent can use timezone: str Describes the input as a string pytz.timezone(timezone) Looks up the timezone rules for that identifier datetime.datetime.now(tz) Reads the current time in that timezone using your computer's clock .strftime(...) Formats the result as readable text return ... Supplies the result to the caller except Exception ... Returns an error message if the input or operation fails

Timezone names identify regions, not fixed offsets. Some regions change offset during daylight saving time. Use Asia/Tokyo for your first test. The function cannot correct an inaccurate computer clock.

docs.title: B. Test it without the agent
docs.text:
With the app stopped and the template's virtual environment still active:

  1. In your code editor, choose New File.
  2. Paste the following code into the new file.
  3. Save it as check_time.py inside your existing First_agent_template folder, next to app.py.
from app import get_current_time_in_timezone

print(get_current_time_in_timezone(timezone="Asia/Tokyo"))
print(get_current_time_in_timezone(timezone="Not/A_Real_Zone"))

In the terminal, make sure you are in First_agent_template with (.venv) active, then run:

python check_time.py

The first line should report Tokyo's date and time. The second should start with Error fetching time. The second test checks how invalid input is handled; it is not a successful time lookup. Neither call uses Groq or needs a key. Importing app defines the tools without launching the chat.

Checkpoint: compare the valid result with a clock set to Tokyo. The invalid-timezone error on the second line is intentional. If the valid Tokyo call fails, fix it before testing through the agent.

If Python says it cannot open check_time.py, confirm that you saved it beside app.py and that the terminal is in that folder. dir on Windows or ls on Mac should list both files. If an ImportError names the time function, check that you kept the function in app.py and saved the file.

docs.title: C. Register it with the agent
docs.text:
If get_current_time_in_timezone is already in your tools list, leave it there and go to Step D. Otherwise, in the original starter's app.py, find tools=[final_answer] inside CodeAgent(...) and replace that argument only with:

tools=[final_answer, get_current_time_in_timezone],

Keep the leading indentation and trailing comma. There should be only one tools= argument. Do not write get_current_time_in_timezone() here: you are registering the capability, not calling it during startup.

Save, run python app.py, enter your Groq key, and refresh the local chat page.

docs.title: D. Ask for a real tool call
docs.text:
Send in the chat:

Use get_current_time_in_timezone with Asia/Tokyo. Report the returned time and say where it came from.

Click Used tool python_interpreter, then Execution Logs inside it to reveal the returned value. You can also inspect the terminal. A possible action is:

result = get_current_time_in_timezone(timezone="Asia/Tokyo")
print(result)

This is illustrative output to recognize, not another block to paste into app.py. The model may use different variable names or call final_answer within the same block.

Checkpoint: find the function call, the returned date/time, and a final answer consistent with it. A statement such as “It is 10:00 in Tokyo” without execution evidence is not enough.

If the direct test works but the agent reports an undefined function, check the registration, spelling, saved file, and restart. If it ignores the function, repeat the explicit tool request in a freshly restarted app.

docs.title: 4. Explore the search tool
docs.text: Goal: let the agent retrieve search results, use them in an answer, and distinguish source evidence from unsupported claims.

docs.title: A. Understand what this tool returns
docs.text:
WebSearchTool is a small adapter supplied in our template’s tools/web_search.py. It connects smolagents to the maintained ddgs Python package, with DuckDuckGo explicitly selected as the search service. The agent sees the name web_search. Its input is one text argument, query. Its output contains result titles, links, and short snippets.

The Python tool contacts a search service. Groq generates the agent's actions and answer; it does not perform this search itself. This starter's search integration requires no separate search API key, but the service can still fail or limit requests.

Search is not full-page reading. This tool returns search-result snippets; it does not fetch and read the full contents of each linked page. When the agent summarizes results, it may only have seen those snippets. You will open a source yourself to verify it. Automatically reading pages would require another tool and is outside the two-tool core practical.

docs.title: B. Test search directly before using the LLM
docs.text:
Stop the app with Control + C if it is running; leave the template's .venv active.

  1. In your code editor, choose New File.
  2. Paste the following code into it.
  3. Save it as check_search.py inside First_agent_template, next to app.py and check_time.py.
from tools.web_search import WebSearchTool

search_tool = WebSearchTool(max_results=3)
print("Agent-facing name:", search_tool.name)
print(search_tool(query="Python official documentation tutorial"))

Run from the First_agent_template folder in your activated terminal:

python check_search.py

This uses the search service directly, without a Groq request or key. It lets you check search connectivity independently of the LLM.

max_results=3 requests up to three results. We use a small number to keep the result readable and reduce how much search text is sent to the model later. It does not limit the number of search calls an agent can make.

Expect the name web_search, followed by a Search Results heading and entries containing a title, URL, and snippet. Exact results and order vary. A shortened illustration, not a live result, is:

Agent-facing name: web_search
## Search Results

[The Python Tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/)
A short search-result description would appear here.

Checkpoint: at least one relevant result is returned and its link opens. If Python cannot open check_search.py, check the file's name, saved location, and current terminal folder as in Step 3B. For a search-service error, use the troubleshooting table below before changing the model or API key.

docs.title: C. Register the search instance
docs.text:
If your tools list already contains WebSearchTool(max_results=3), keep it and go to Step D. Otherwise, the starter already imports WebSearchTool from tools.web_search near the top of app.py. The import alone does not register it. Find your existing tools= argument and replace it with:

tools=[
    final_answer,
    get_current_time_in_timezone,
    WebSearchTool(max_results=3),
],

Indent this block to match the other arguments inside CodeAgent(...). Keep the surrounding constructor and all its other arguments.

Expression Meaning WebSearchTool The class imported into your app WebSearchTool(max_results=3) A configured instance that can be registered web_search(query="...") The name and call the agent uses in generated Python

Do not rename the class to web_search in your import. The tool supplies that agent-facing name itself. Open tools/web_search.py to see the adapter: DDGS(timeout=15).text(..., backend="duckduckgo") sends the search; the adapter formats the returned dictionaries for the agent. The DDGS package documentation describes its backend options.

Save and restart with python app.py, paste your key, and refresh the local browser page.

docs.title: D. Give the agent a specific search task
docs.text:
Send:

Use web_search to find the official Python tutorial. Return one relevant title and URL from the results, and briefly explain why that source matches. Say if you only saw a search snippet.

This asks for an observable action and a bounded answer. For the first test, avoid a broad task such as “research everything about AI,” which can lead to many calls and a hard-to-check answer.

The trace may contain code like:

results = web_search(query="Python official documentation tutorial")
print(results)

The model can then use those results in another step, or finish in the same step. python_interpreter in the trace is expected: CodeAgent runs Python that calls the registered search tool.

docs.title: E. Follow the evidence into the final answer
docs.text:
Check these in order:

Open Used tool python_interpreter → Execution Logs to inspect returned search entries.

  1. Action: does generated code actually call web_search with a relevant query?
  2. Observation: did that call return search results, rather than an error?
  3. Answer: is the cited URL present in the observation?
  4. Source: open the URL in your browser. Does its domain and page content support the claim?

For the Python example, the official documentation uses docs.python.org. A good-looking title alone does not establish who published a page. For current information, also inspect publication or update dates; a page appearing in search does not make it current.

If the final answer claims details absent from the snippets, verify them on the actual page. Do not treat an invented quotation or a model-generated link as retrieved evidence. Text returned by a search is source material, not an instruction to change the agent's task.

Checkpoint: you can point to a search call, one returned result, and a supported statement in the final answer. An error is useful for diagnosis but does not complete this checkpoint.

docs.title: F. Improve one query yourself
docs.text:
Keep the working code and change only the chat request. Choose a topic, then compare a broad query with a more specific query containing the subject and source you want. For example, compare “Python” with “Python documentation defining functions.”

Record which result is useful and why. This small exercise is about judging retrieved evidence, not copying a predetermined answer. Each agent run may use multiple model requests, so run the examples one at a time and respect usage limits.

docs.title: G. Diagnose search failures
docs.text:
Search availability check

A fresh Mac test exposed failures in the original duckduckgo_search integration. The current starter uses ddgs==9.16.0 with an explicit DuckDuckGo backend. Direct search and a real agent search returned official Python sources, but later searches returned no results even after rephrasing. Search is intermittent. In one combined run the model supplied a correct-looking URL from memory after search failed; that did not pass the search checkpoint.

Symptom Meaning and next action ModuleNotFoundError mentioning ddgs Activate the template's .venv and run python -m pip install -r requirements.txt from its folder. Then rerun check_search.py. Warning that the package was renamed to ddgs You are using the older built-in search tool. Use the updated starter’s tools/web_search.py, import WebSearchTool from that file, and reinstall the updated requirements. Do not just rename the old import from smolagents. No results found Shorten or rephrase the query, then try the direct test once. Empty results are not evidence that the information does not exist. Timeout, connection error, or search-service block Check internet access and whether the search site opens in your browser. A browser working does not guarantee automated requests are allowed. Retry later or on another permitted network. Search-service rate limit Pause and retry later. Do not repeatedly restart or send rapid retries. A new Groq key cannot resolve a search-service limit. Groq 429 during the agent test Read the terminal: “Request too large” needs a smaller output budget or shorter input; other exhausted limits need the indicated reset. See the setup troubleshooting table. A successful direct search does not prove Groq has remaining capacity. web_search undefined in generated code Check that a search-tool instance is in tools, save, and restart the app. Direct search works, but the agent does not call it Use the explicit prompt in Step D, verify registration, and retry with fresh agent memory by restarting the app. Search returns results, but the answer gives another URL Compare the answer with the observation and request a URL actually present in the results.

If external search remains unavailable, continue reading the trace explanation and return to the live checkpoint later. Label the search test incomplete; do not replace it with invented results.

docs.title: 5. Verify the two core tools
docs.text:
Time and search are a useful first pair: time provides an easily checked local result, while search introduces an external service and source evaluation. Neither requires adding another API key in this starter. Search can still be blocked or rate-limited independently of Groq.

Test each separately before combining them. For a combined test, ask:

Get the current time in Asia/Tokyo using the time tool, then search for the official Python documentation. Give me a source link actually returned by web_search. If search fails, say that it failed; do not substitute a link from memory.

Inspect the trace for both calls and their successful outputs. Compare the time with a trusted clock and open the returned documentation link. The link must occur in the search observation, even if you already know it is correct. If the agent skips a tool, ask explicitly for it and inspect the next run. Do not count a fabricated time or a link supplied from memory as successful execution. This prompt makes the requirement clearer but does not replace checking the evidence yourself.

final_answer remains in the tools list as the framework's completion mechanism; it is separate from the two capabilities you are learning to enable.

Image generation has been removed from this adaptation. There is no image tool to register or image-service setup to complete.

docs.title: 6. Optional: create your own tool
docs.text:
You choose the purpose of your tool. The example below uses a tiny invented Mordor-style glossary to show where the code and descriptions go. These demo words are not authentic translations, and this is not a general translator. You can use another topic for your own tool.

The process is write → describe → test directly → register → ask the agent → inspect execution. A description tells the model what your function does; you must still implement that behavior.

docs.title: A. Write the function and its description
docs.text:
Stop the app with Control + C. In app.py, find the optional @tool / my_custom_tool placeholder above main(). Replace that entire decorated function, including its old docstring and raise NotImplementedError(...), with this example. Keep the existing timezone function and the rest of the app.

@tool  # Make the function's name, description, and inputs available to smolagents.
def translate_to_mordor(text: str) -> str:
    """Translate one supported English word using an invented Mordor-style demo glossary.

    Args:
        text: One English word to translate: hello, friend, or goodbye.
    """
    glossary = {"hello": "mor", "friend": "dur", "goodbye": "nak"}  # Invented demo words.
    word = text.strip().lower()  # Ignore surrounding spaces and capital letters.
    if word not in glossary:
        return "Unsupported word. Choose hello, friend, or goodbye."
    return glossary[word]  # Return the dictionary result; no model or online translator is called.
Code Meaning translate_to_mordor Name the agent will use to call the tool text: str The input is a string -> str The result is a string First sentence inside triple quotes Tool description: what it does and when it is useful Args: / text: Description of the input the model should supply glossary, lookup, and return Actual Python implementation

Where do you change the description? Edit the docstring under def, not the chat message or prompts.yaml. Describe the real capability and its limits. This function supports only three words, so its description says so.

docs.title: B. Test the function before the agent calls it
docs.text:
In your editor, create a new file named check_my_tool.py beside app.py, paste the following, and save it. Keep the app stopped and the template's .venv active.

from app import translate_to_mordor  # Import the new function; do not launch the chat.

print(translate_to_mordor(text="Hello"))  # Normal input; capital letters are accepted.
print(translate_to_mordor(text="unknown"))  # Unsupported input checks the function's limit.

In the terminal, from First_agent_template, run:

python check_my_tool.py

Expected output:

mor
Unsupported word. Choose hello, friend, or goodbye.

This is a direct Python test. It does not use Groq or require a key. If you choose a different tool, change the import and inputs to match your function, and write down expected results before running it. Fix direct-test failures before testing through the agent.

docs.title: C. Connect the tool to CodeAgent
docs.text:
Inside main(), find CodeAgent(...). Add your function's name to its existing tools list, keeping the time, search, and final-answer tools:

tools=[
    final_answer,
    get_current_time_in_timezone,
    WebSearchTool(max_results=3),
    translate_to_mordor,  # ADDED: allow the agent to call the new function.
],

Register a decorated function by name: translate_to_mordor, without parentheses. Writing translate_to_mordor(...) here would call it during startup instead of registering it. WebSearchTool(max_results=3) uses parentheses because it creates a tool-class instance. Keep only one tools= argument inside CodeAgent(...).

You do not need another .py file for the tool itself when its definition is in app.py. check_my_tool.py is only the test script.

docs.title: D. Restart and ask for a tool call
docs.text:
Save app.py, run python app.py, enter your Groq key when prompted, and refresh the chat page. Send:

Use translate_to_mordor to translate the word Hello using the demo glossary. Report the returned value.

CodeAgent supplies the model with your registered tool's name and docstring. The model can generate an action such as:

translated = translate_to_mordor(text="Hello")
print(translated)
final_answer(translated)

This is an example of generated action code to recognize in the trace; do not paste it into your function definition. The local executor runs the call. If another step is needed, CodeAgent supplies the result or error to the model, which can continue toward an answer. You do not write that action loop yourself as you did in the dummy exercise.

docs.title: E. Check that the new tool actually ran
docs.text:
Open Used tool python_interpreter → Execution Logs. Find the translate_to_mordor call, the returned mor, and a final answer consistent with that result. The model saying “I translated it” without an executed call is insufficient.

Then ask for an unsupported word. The answer should report the function's limit instead of inventing a translation. If the function works directly but the agent test fails, check the saved file, registration, exact function name, docstring, generated arguments, and restart. Tool choice is made by the model, so inspect the trace even when you explicitly name the tool.

docs.title: If you later put the tool in a separate file
docs.text:
For your first tool, keeping it above main() in app.py is simplest. If you choose to organize it as tools/mordor.py, move the complete decorated function there and add this import at the top of that file:

from smolagents import tool

Then import the function near the top of app.py:

from tools.mordor import translate_to_mordor

Keep its registration in CodeAgent's tools list. Remove the duplicate definition from app.py, and update the direct test to import from tools.mordor. Importing loads the tool into your program; registering exposes it to the agent. The folder name tools/ alone does not connect anything.

For the interface details, see the smolagents 1.13.0 tools guide. For Python parameters, returns, and docstrings, see Python's function guide.

docs.title: 7. Inspect instructions and settings
docs.text:
A prompt is text sent as part of a model request. The system instructions in prompts.yaml describe available tools and the expected response structure. They guide generation; they do not execute functions or train the model. The template placeholders are filled with information such as tool descriptions when the agent builds its instructions.

Open prompts.yaml and locate the instructions. Compare one formatting instruction with a response in your trace. See the template explanation for how those instructions reach the model. If experimenting, back up the file and preserve its YAML indentation and template placeholders.

In app.py, locate the model identifier and max_steps. Keep working settings for the first run. max_steps limits the action loop, while max_tokens limits the output allowance of an individual completion. Neither grants extra API credits or guarantees a correct answer. Experiments with other models remain possible, subject to access and library compatibility.

docs.title: 8. Demonstrate the result
docs.text:
Demonstrate timezone lookup and web search, showing each call, observation, and final answer. If you completed the optional custom tool, demonstrate that too. Use errors to revise your implementation or description and retry.

Demonstrate the local app. Publishing a Space is the environment-specific exception and is not required. A temporary public link, if deliberately enabled, uses the app owner's credentials and is not permanent hosting.

docs.title: 9. Complete the local practical
docs.text: Review the completion checks. The two quick quizzes appear in the foundations lesson; there is no final-quiz or certificate requirement.

docs.title: Prepare your computer
docs.text: Complete this setup in Week 1 after the concepts and before the Dummy Agent exercise. You only need Python and a Groq key at this stage. You will download the full agent template after the three dummy stages.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Open Command Prompt, then run each command separately:

winget install --exact --id Python.Python.3.11

Accept the installer prompts, close and reopen Command Prompt, then check:

py -3.11 --version

If winget is unavailable, open the Python 3.11.9 release page, scroll to Files, and download the Windows installer (64-bit) for an x64 PC. Run it, enable Add python.exe to PATH and the Python launcher, finish installation, then reopen Command Prompt and retry py -3.11 --version. Use Command Prompt, not PowerShell, for this guide's Windows commands.

docs.title: Mac
docs.text:
Open Terminal. If Homebrew is installed, run:

brew install python@3.11

If Homebrew is missing, follow its installation instructions, including the final setup instructions, then retry.

Check the installations:

python3.11 --version

Checkpoint: You see Python 3.11.x. On Mac, python3 may still point to an older version; this is fine. Use python3.11 below.

docs.title: 2. Create a folder for the dummy exercise
docs.text: Open your terminal and run the commands for your operating system, one at a time.

docs.title: Windows — Command Prompt
docs.text:
mkdir "%USERPROFILE%\agent-course\dummy-agent"
cd /d "%USERPROFILE%\agent-course\dummy-agent"
py -3.11 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat
python --version

docs.title: Mac — Terminal
docs.text:
mkdir -p ~/agent-course/dummy-agent
cd ~/agent-course/dummy-agent
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python --version

A virtual environment is a separate set of Python libraries for this exercise. Creating .venv makes that environment; activating it makes the terminal use it. Keep the dummy exercise and the Week 2 template in their own environments.

If the folder already exists, enter it instead of creating it again. A virtual environment only needs creating once.

Checkpoint: Your terminal shows (.venv) and Python 3.11.x. Keep this window open.

docs.title: 3. Install the model client
docs.text:
On either system:

python -m pip install "openai>=1.0,<3"

Wait for the normal terminal prompt to return without a final error. The library connects to Groq's compatible API; you do not need an OpenAI account.

docs.title: 4. Create your Groq API key
docs.text: Sign up or sign in to Groq Console using your own account. The free plan has usage limits; see Groq's limits.

docs.title: A. Open the key page
docs.text:
1. In your browser, sign in to Groq Console.
  2. Open API Keys in the console navigation, or use the direct API Keys link.
  3. Click Create API Key.
  4. Enter a descriptive name such as agents-course in the name field. If an expiration choice is offered, choose one that covers your course sessions.
  5. Confirm creation using the dialog's create/submit button.
  6. Copy the generated secret key and keep it in a password manager so you can retrieve it at startup. Do not share it with classmates or paste it into this guide, source code, or chat.

The name agents-course is only a label. The generated secret value is the actual key. The console's labels may vary; Groq's official quickstart also links to key creation.

Checkpoint: You have your own Groq key ready. Creating a key does not choose a model or prove that a model request will succeed.

The dummy script will ask you to paste this key into a hidden terminal prompt. The full agent will use the same key later. Do not put it in your Python files.

docs.title: 5. Continue to the dummy exercise
docs.text: If needed, finish the lessons and quick quizzes, then follow the three dummy stages. At this point you do not need app.py, Gradio, or the full agent ZIP.

docs.title: Restart the dummy exercise another day
docs.text:
On Windows:

cd /d "%USERPROFILE%\agent-course\dummy-agent"
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat

On Mac:

cd ~/agent-course/dummy-agent
source .venv/bin/activate

Run python dummy_agent.py after you have created that file during the exercise. Paste your key when prompted. Output appears in the terminal, not a browser chat.

docs.title: Quick quizzes and completion
docs.text:
This adaptation uses only the two original Hugging Face quick quizzes. They open on the external site and retain its questions and feedback.

When Activity After the introduction to agents Quick Quiz 1 After models, messages, and tools Quick Quiz 2

The final quiz requires account access in the reported setup and is excluded from this course route. No Hugging Face certification or final-quiz submission is required. The local lessons and practical do not depend on external lesson pages.

If a quick quiz fails to load, open it in a regular browser tab and reload. Continue with the local exercise while the external activity is unavailable. This guide does not record scores or award an official Hugging Face certificate.

docs.title: Finish the practical
docs.text:
For Week 1, use the dummy-agent completion checks.

For Week 2, after building your tools, check that you can:

  • Identify a real timezone-tool call and its returned time.
  • Identify a real web-search call and open a relevant returned source.
  • Explain the roles of the model, Groq, smolagents, and local functions.
  • Distinguish a tool error from a successful observation.

These are practical completion checks, not a replacement final quiz. A custom tool is optional; image generation is not included.

Also demonstrate a successful template response, show how to stop and restart the app, and explain the difference between the manual dummy loop and CodeAgent. Record unavailable live checkpoints as incomplete and return to them later. See the two-week course route.

docs.title: Download and run the first-agent template
docs.text:
Begin Week 2 after finishing the three dummy stages first. Then use this page to download the complete template, prepare its own environment, and start the app. CodeAgent will manage the model/action/observation loop that you assembled manually in the dummy exercise.

Your earlier basic setup already provided Python 3.11 and your Groq key. This page continues from that setup. Your computer runs the app and tools; Groq provides the remote model, so you still need an internet connection.

Follow only the commands for your operating system. For help with terminals, folders, and editing, see Before you start.

docs.title: 1. Have your Groq API key ready
docs.text:
Use the same Groq API key you prepared during basic setup. Have it ready to paste into the hidden terminal prompt when you start the app in Step 8. You do not need to create another account or key.

If you have not prepared your key yet, complete the linked setup step before continuing.

docs.title: 2. Use your existing Python installation
docs.text:
Use Python 3.11 from basic setup. The new environment in Step 4 will check its version. If you have not installed it yet, complete the Python setup step before continuing.

If your dummy exercise is still running, stop it with Control + C. If its virtual environment is active (the prompt shows (.venv)), run deactivate before switching to the template folder.

docs.title: 3. Download the agent template
docs.text:
Complete agent template

One ZIP containing app.py, the interface, tools, instructions, and library requirements. “Groq starter” and “agent template” refer to this same download. It includes no API key or virtual environment.

Download agent template (.zip)

  1. Click Download agent template (.zip) above.
  2. Extract the ZIP: double-click it on Mac, or right-click and choose Extract All on Windows.
  3. Locate the extracted folder containing app.py, Gradio_UI.py, requirements.txt, prompts.yaml, and tools. Its name is First_agent_template; it also includes STUDENT_TASKS.md with the tasks you will complete.
  4. Move First_agent_template into the agent-course folder you created during basic setup. If a First_agent_template folder already exists, keep a backup before replacing it.
  5. Open a terminal and enter the project folder:

Windows — Command Prompt

cd /d "%USERPROFILE%\agent-course\First_agent_template"

Mac — Terminal

cd ~/agent-course/First_agent_template

Do not work inside an unopened ZIP. If extraction created two nested folders with the same name, use the inner folder containing app.py.

Checkpoint: Run dir on Windows or ls on Mac. Confirm app.py and requirements.txt are listed.

docs.title: 4. Create a virtual environment
docs.text: Create a new environment inside First_agent_template so its libraries stay separate from the dummy exercise. Run these commands once, after entering the folder in Step 3.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
py -3.11 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat
python --version

docs.title: Mac
docs.text:
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python --version

Checkpoint: The prompt starts with (.venv) and Python reports version 3.11.x. Keep using this terminal window.

docs.title: 5. Install the libraries
docs.text:
On either operating system:

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

Wait for installation to finish and the prompt to return. Download progress bars are normal.

Checkpoint: There is no final ERROR message. You may see Successfully installed or Requirement already satisfied. Do not enter the next command while installation is still running.

Use the requirements.txt included in the Groq ZIP. It includes the openai client library, used here to connect to Groq through its compatible API; you do not need an OpenAI account.

docs.title: 6. Keep the supplied model settings
docs.text:
The template already connects to Groq using these settings in app.py:

model_id="qwen/qwen3.8-27b",
api_base="https://api.groq.com/openai/v1",

It also sets reasoning_effort="none" for code-agent responses. Leave these settings unchanged for the first run. Keep your API key out of the source code; the app will ask for it at startup.

docs.title: 7. Confirm local-only sharing
docs.text:
The Groq starter already uses share=False in Gradio_UI.py and binds the app to 127.0.0.1. No edit is required.

If checking an older copy, find demo.launch in Gradio_UI.py and confirm it contains share=False. A public link would allow other people to send requests using the running app's Groq credentials.

docs.title: 8. Start the agent
docs.text:
python app.py

Terminal first asks:

Paste your Groq API key (hidden):

Paste your key and press Enter/Return. Nothing appears while pasting; that is normal. The app then prints:

Using Groq: qwen/qwen3.8-27b

The key stays in memory while the app runs; it is not saved. If you separately configured GROQ_API_KEY, the app uses that value instead of prompting. Never print or share it.

Wait for output similar to:

Running on local URL: http://127.0.0.1:7860

Open the exact address shown in your browser. Keep the terminal running.

The address goes in your browser's address bar, not the agent chat. If the terminal prints a different port, use that port. The command will not return to its normal prompt while the app is running; that is expected.

docs.title: 9. Test the connection to the LLM
docs.text:
Send:

What is 12 multiplied by 8?

Look for a final answer containing 96. You may also see generated Python code and a python_interpreter step.

Checkpoint: A model-generated answer confirms that your key, account access, endpoint, and model worked for this request. Opening the chat page alone only checks the interface. If the answer fails, use the troubleshooting table below.

The download includes working time and search implementations, but only final_answer is registered initially. You will test and register the two supplied tools in the tools practical. Until then, the agent cannot use the supplied web_search tool. It may still answer from model knowledge or produce a URL; neither proves that it searched.

docs.title: 10. Check your usage limits
docs.text: A single chat message can trigger several model requests. Check Groq's usage limits and avoid rapid repeated submissions. API keys authenticate requests; input and output tokens measure the text used. See the template explanation for the output budget and request settings.

docs.title: 11. Stop and restart
docs.text:
To stop the app, click the terminal and press Control + C.

To restart another day, open a new terminal and run:

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
cd /d "%USERPROFILE%\agent-course\First_agent_template"
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat
python app.py

docs.title: Mac
docs.text:
cd ~/agent-course/First_agent_template
source .venv/bin/activate
python app.py

You do not need to reinstall libraries. Paste your Groq key again when prompted, then open the printed local URL.

docs.title: Model connection problems
docs.text:
Problem Next step Python is the wrong version Activate the Python 3.11 environment from Step 4. app.py or requirements.txt cannot be found Enter the extracted First_agent_template folder. ModuleNotFoundError: openai Activate .venv and rerun Step 5. No Groq key entered Restart and paste your key into the hidden prompt. 400 / tool_use_failed / “Tool choice is none” Use the current starter's app.py and prompts.yaml, stop the old process, and restart. It now selects Qwen rather than GPT-OSS and explicitly requests Python text. If it repeats, check Groq’s tool-call behavior and the model ID against the current download. Do not enable native tools blindly: this exercise expects Python text. 401 / invalid API key Use the full Groq key, not its label or an HF token. Check it has not expired or been revoked. 403 / access denied Check your Groq account/project's model access and any organization restrictions. 429 / Request too large Read the limit named in the terminal. For output tokens, lower max_tokens in app.py (the current starter uses 512), save, and restart. For input tokens, restart to clear chat history or shorten the prompt. Waiting alone does not fix an oversized request. 429 / rate limit (usage exhausted) Follow the retry interval. Free-tier limits apply to both requests and tokens. Avoid rapid repeated messages. 404 / model unavailable Compare model_id with Groq’s supported models and check your console’s model permissions. Model IDs must match exactly. HF router 402 / no credits You are still running the old HF model connection. Stop that app and use the Groq starter; buying HF credits is not required for this version. Old NoneType token-count crash Confirm you are using the updated Gradio_UI.py from the starter ZIP. Page opens but chat fails Read the model error in the terminal; the page alone does not test API access. Connection error or timeout Check internet access and Groq service availability, then retry once. The current starter uses a 30-second timeout per attempt and at most two automatic retries; do not repeatedly submit messages while it is waiting. Browser cannot connect Keep the app running and use its printed local URL. Port already in use Stop the older app process before launching again.

For help, share your operating system, command, and final error lines. Exclude credentials.

docs.title: Common editing mistakes
docs.text:
Message or symptom What to check IndentationError Restore the leading spaces around your edit. Use the original file or backup as a reference. SyntaxError Check for a missing comma, quote, square bracket, or parenthesis in the edited lines. NameError after adding a tool Check the function name's spelling, that it is defined above the agent, and that the file was saved. File appears to be app.py.txt Save from a code editor as app.py; do not add .txt. Changes have no effect Save the file, stop and restart the app, then refresh its browser page. Terminal shows >>> Type exit() to return to the command prompt before running shell commands.

Completion check: You can start the app, obtain an LLM response, explain where the model runs, and stop the app.

Next: Understand smolagents and what the template does, then build your agent’s tools.

docs.title: Understand smolagents and the template
docs.text: Read this after your first successful response and before adding tools. Keep app.py open beside the guide. By the end, you should be able to explain which component generates text, which executes an action, and where to add your own capability.

docs.title: 1. What is smolagents?
docs.text:
smolagents is a Python library for building agents, developed by Hugging Face. A library is reusable code you import into your program. Here, it provides the machinery for asking a model what to do, executing an action, recording the result, and continuing toward an answer. Its CodeAgent represents actions as Python code. See the smolagents introduction for version 1.13.0, which matches this starter.

In the dummy exercise, you assembled messages, called the LLM, ran a weather function, and returned its result. The template lets a framework manage that sequence. You still choose the model, provide tools, and check the outcome.

We continue using Hugging Face's library and course material while using Groq's API for model requests. Installing smolagents does not require hosting a Space or buying Hugging Face inference credits for this configuration.

docs.title: 2. Which component does what?
docs.text:
An agent in this project is the complete arrangement of model, instructions, available actions, and execution loop.

Component Job in this template Runs where? Qwen model Generates the next response, including proposed Python actions Remotely, through Groq Groq API Receives authenticated requests and returns model output Groq's service OpenAIServerModel Adapts smolagents messages to the compatible API Your Python process CodeAgent Coordinates model requests, Python execution, and observations Your Python process A registered tool Performs a capability you make available, such as looking up a time Called locally; some tools contact another service Gradio Provides the browser chat interface A local web server plus your browser

The word “OpenAI” in OpenAIServerModel names an API-compatible connection class. In this template its address points to Groq, and its key is a Groq key. You do not need an OpenAI account.

The time tool reads your computer's clock and applies a timezone. The search tool sends a request to an external search service. Both are Python capabilities; their sources of information differ.

docs.title: 3. From a message to an answer
docs.text:
The arrows below show the two-way flow. The same local agent makes each model request.

Browser chat
    ↓ user message
Gradio → CodeAgent on your computer
              ↓ instructions + task + earlier observations
         Groq → Qwen model
              ↓ model response containing Python code
         Local Python execution
              ↓ result or error recorded as an observation
         CodeAgent → another model request if needed
              ↓ final_answer(...) completes the task
Browser displays the result

For example, after you register the timezone tool, an action could contain:

current_time = get_current_time_in_timezone("Asia/Tokyo")
print(current_time)

The model generates that code. The local executor runs it. Its output becomes an observation that can be included in the next request. The model might then generate final_answer(...) to finish. It can also call a tool and finish within one code block, so every task does not have the same number of steps.

This explains why one chat message can consume multiple API requests. It also explains why a model saying “I checked the time” is insufficient evidence: look for the executed call and its result.

docs.title: What CodeAgent handles automatically
docs.text:
Yes: CodeAgent manages the action–observation loop for you. The model chooses proposed actions; the framework runs the generated Python locally and records the result.

Responsibility Who handles it? Write the tool's function and describe its inputs You Register the function in tools=[...] You Supply registered tool names and descriptions in the model's instructions CodeAgent Choose whether to use a tool and generate Python arguments The model Execute the Python, call the tool, and record output or errors CodeAgent's local executor Include observations in later requests when another step is needed CodeAgent Generate code calling final_answer(...) The model Finish the run and return the final result CodeAgent

For a request such as “Use the time tool for Asia/Tokyo,” CodeAgent supplies the task and the registered tools to the model, executes the proposed call, and continues if needed. The run can end with a final answer, reach its step limit, or stop because of an error. Registration and automatic execution do not guarantee correct choices or correct answers.

The dummy exercise asked you to inspect an action and call a hard-coded function yourself. Here, CodeAgent handles that execution loop. A simple Python calculation such as 12 * 8 uses the built-in executor; a real search needs a registered search tool. Neither a generated “Thought” nor a function name appearing in text proves execution.

Follow how tools are connected and selected and the new-tool example in the practical to see where each part is edited.

docs.title: 4. What does the downloaded template provide?
docs.text:
The template is a starting program with the connection and interface already assembled. It can answer a simple question immediately. The student version deliberately leaves the two core tools (time and web search) unregistered. The unfinished custom tool is an optional extension. Image generation has been removed.

File Purpose What you do with it app.py Defines tools, configures Groq, creates the agent, and launches the interface Main file for your practical edits Gradio_UI.py Passes chat messages to the agent and displays steps, answers, and errors Read to trace the interface; no edits needed for the tasks prompts.yaml Stores text templates for instructions and response formatting Inspect after the basic tool tasks tools/web_search.py Adapts the DDGS client to a smolagents tool, using the DuckDuckGo backend Register its WebSearchTool class in the practical tools/final_answer.py Defines the final-answer tool used by this starter Keep it available requirements.txt Lists Python packages and version constraints Install with the supplied setup command STUDENT_TASKS.md Lists the tool activities and completion checks Use alongside the practical .venv/ Holds your locally installed Python environment Created during setup; not part of the downloadable code

The template contains neither the model's weights nor your API key. Downloading it does not download an LLM onto your laptop.

docs.title: Imports and function definitions
docs.text:
from smolagents import ... makes library components available to this program. Defining get_current_time_in_timezone creates a callable tool, but does not fetch the time at startup. Similarly, importing WebSearchTool does not perform a web search.

The custom placeholder raises NotImplementedError if called. This is intentional: implement it before registering it. The initial app runs because it does not expose that placeholder to the agent.

docs.title: main() and the startup guard
docs.text:
At the bottom of the file:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Running python app.py triggers main(). Importing app from a tool-test script defines its functions without launching the chat. That lets you test your own tool independently.

docs.title: The key prompt
docs.text:
main() checks the GROQ_API_KEY environment variable first. If it is empty, getpass(...) asks for a key without displaying it. The key authorizes API requests. It is different from the input and output tokens that measure text usage.

The app does not save a key entered at the prompt. You enter it again after restarting unless you configured the environment variable separately.

docs.title: The model connection
docs.text:
These are the working starter's settings, shown for explanation rather than as a replacement block:

model = OpenAIServerModel(
    model_id="qwen/qwen3.8-27b",
    api_base="https://api.groq.com/openai/v1",
    api_key=api_key,
    client_kwargs={"timeout": 30, "max_retries": 2},
    max_tokens=512,
    temperature=0.5,
    reasoning_effort="none",
)
Setting Meaning model_id Exact identifier of the model requested from the service api_base Address to which the client sends requests api_key Credential supplied at startup max_tokens Maximum output per completion. We start with 512 tokens for short exercises; this must fit your account allowance and is not a daily usage budget. client_kwargs Each network attempt has a 30-second timeout; up to two automatic retries handle temporary failures and short rate-limit waits. Longer limits can still stop the run. temperature Sampling setting affecting variation; it does not measure accuracy reasoning_effort A model-specific option configured here to disable the model's separate reasoning mode

Keep these settings for the initial practical. Changing the model may change supported options and response format. It does not automatically give you a larger usage allowance.

docs.title: Instructions and agent construction
docs.text:
The program reads prompts.yaml next to app.py, then constructs CodeAgent. The important arguments are:

model=model,
tools=[final_answer],
max_steps=6,
prompt_templates=prompt_templates,

model selects the connection. tools supplies the explicit capabilities available to the agent. max_steps limits its action-loop iterations for a task; it is not a guarantee of success or an exact cap on total API calls. prompt_templates supplies instructions for those interactions. The versioned agent reference documents these parameters and the distinction between Python-code agents and JSON tool-calling agents.

The starter also supplies several optional settings as None, including planning and managed-agent metadata. You do not need to change them to complete the tools exercise. verbosity_level=1 controls logging detail.

docs.title: Launching the interface
docs.text:
GradioUI(agent).launch(server_name="127.0.0.1") starts the local interface. Starting this server does not itself request an answer from the LLM. Sending a chat message triggers agent.run(...) in Gradio_UI.py.

The URL is local, but model requests still travel over the internet. Stopping the Python process stops the app. Refreshing a browser page does not reload changed Python files; restart the program after code edits.

docs.title: 6. How does a function become a tool?
docs.text:
A useful function must exist, describe its inputs and purpose, and be registered with the agent.

@tool
def get_current_time_in_timezone(timezone: str) -> str:

@tool is a Python decorator: it wraps the function with information smolagents can use. The type hints describe the expected argument and return types. The docstring describes the capability and its arguments. These descriptions help the model select a function and construct inputs; they do not implement its behavior. The versioned tools guide explains this interface.

Registering the existing function means adding its name to tools. Use the name without calling it: calling it yourself would produce a result immediately instead of registering the capability. WebSearchTool() is different syntax because it creates an instance of a supplied tool class.

For the optional custom-tool extension, you must still write the function body and verify its return value. Accurate documentation cannot repair an incorrect calculation. A sensible test order is direct function call → registration → agent request → trace inspection. See the optional new-tool walkthrough for a complete example with a description, a test file, registration, and a chat request.

docs.title: 7. Why final_answer is already included
docs.text:
In the template, final_answer = FinalAnswerTool() creates the object registered under that name. Generated Python such as final_answer(96) signals completion and supplies the result to display. This function does not make an additional LLM request on its own.

That is why a greeting can show a python_interpreter step even when it needs no search or external lookup: this CodeAgent may execute a small Python block that calls final_answer.

The initial agent can use its Python executor for simple calculations even though its explicit tools list contains only the final-answer tool. Registering search or your timezone function adds those specific capabilities.

docs.title: 8. Read the trace and understand the limits
docs.text:
What you see What it tells you Model commentary or “Thought” Generated explanation; not proof of an action or a complete account of internal reasoning Code The action proposed by the model python_interpreter The framework executing generated Python Observation / execution output Information returned by execution, including possible errors Final answer The reported result; still check it against the observations Input/output token counts Text usage for model requests, not the API key

The UI preserves the agent's history between messages in the running app. Later requests can therefore contain previous steps as context, increasing usage. Restart the app when you want an independent experiment with fresh agent memory. This conversation history is not model training.

An error before a model response suggests a connection, access, request-format, or usage-limit issue. An error while executing code suggests a problem with generated arguments, tool code, registration, or execution permissions. Follow the troubleshooting table for the corresponding layer.

docs.title: 9. Before you start editing
docs.text:
Use these as reading checks, not an additional graded quiz:

  • Explain why importing a search class does not enable searching.
  • Trace one answer from the chat input through an action to the displayed result.
  • Identify the optional custom-tool placeholder and the two core capabilities you need to register.

Start Week 1 with these concepts; local setup follows the reading. Each topic below links directly to its original Hugging Face lesson, where you can follow Alfred’s illustrations and other visual explanations. Our self-contained notes remain below each link. Use this guide for the local Python and Groq practical.

If an original HF activity does not work

Some hands-on activities and playgrounds in the original Hugging Face course may currently be unavailable or may not work with your account or environment. You can still read the explanations and follow Alfred’s illustrations.

If an original HF activity does not load or run, skip that activity and continue reading. You do not need to complete a broken HF playground to proceed with this course.
